title: Jersey to Brooklyn: The Camera at Chichen Itza and the Queen Who Became Isis
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: St. Helier, Jersey: born on the island between two countries
stops.date_confidence: attested. Birth on the Island of Jersey, 4 May 1825, per the standard account; no parish, house, or officiant is named in the sources consulted
stops.campa: Augustus Henry Julian Le Plongeon is born on the fourth of May, 1825, on Jersey in the Channel Islands, a rock of French speech under an English crown. The island makes a boy who will be French to Americans and foreign everywhere else, a man with two languages before he has a trade. Within twenty years he is on the far side of the world with no intention of coming back. Nothing in the reachable record describes the house, the christening, or the mother. The date and the island are what there is.
suggested_refs: The parish registers of St. Helier, Jersey, for May 1825

stops.name: Off the Chilean coast, the wreck
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The shipwreck is reported in the standard account with no month, no vessel name, and no position; the year is derived from his stated age of about nineteen. The coordinate is an open-water approximation off Valparaiso, not a located wreck site
stops.campa: At about nineteen he ships out of Europe for South America and the vessel is lost off the coast of Chile. No reachable source names the ship, the month, or the reef; only that he survives it and comes ashore on a coast where he knows no one. He is fluent in French and English, competent in mathematics and drawing, and carries no capital at all. Whatever plan put him aboard ends in the water, and no letter, diary, or passenger list survives to say what the plan was. He walks into Valparaiso and looks for work.
suggested_refs: Chilean coastal wreck registers for the mid-1840s, not consulted for this file

stops.name: Valparaiso, teaching in the port
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the fact and the place; the sources consulted give no month, and the year follows from the shipwreck
stops.campa: In the port city of Valparaiso he takes a post at a local college teaching mathematics, drawing, and languages. It is the first of the trades he will practice in five countries: teacher, surveyor, photographer, doctor, excavator, none of them held long enough to make him a professional in anyone else's eyes. He stays five years on a coast where ships from every ocean unload, learning the Spanish that will carry him through Peru and Yucatan. Drawing is the skill that pays for everything after.
suggested_refs: The teaching colleges of Valparaiso in the 1840s, before the 1906 earthquake destroyed much of the old port

segments.name: The Gold Country and the Camera

stops.name: San Francisco, into the gold rush as a surveyor
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; no month in the sources consulted. The coordinate is the canonical San Francisco pin used across the corpus, not a located address
stops.campa: In 1849 he leaves Chile for the north, where news out of the American River has emptied every port on the Pacific. He does not dig. He surveys, which in a country being invented at speed is the steadier trade, and he apprentices himself in medicine besides, acquiring a second profession he will practice on and off for sixty years without a degree anyone recognizes. The city he lands in is a few thousand tents and a harbor of ships their crews have walked away from. Men who can run a chain and read an angle are scarce, and he is one of them.
suggested_refs: California land survey records of 1849-1851 for the Sacramento and Feather river districts

stops.name: Marysville, the town drawn on paper
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1850 by the Marysville town history, which names Covillaud, Ramirez, Sampson and Sicard as hiring him to plan the town. The standard Le Plongeon account dates the survey 1851, conflating it with the town's incorporation on 5 February 1851; the contradiction is recorded here, not resolved
stops.campa: Covillaud, Ramirez, Sampson and Sicard hire the French surveyor to lay out a town at the head of navigation on the Feather River. He draws the streets and the blocks and takes his fee in deeds to lots he has just invented, which is how a young man with no money acquires land in a boom. Sold off later, those deeds pay for glass plates, mules and hired labor at Chichen Itza a quarter century afterward. The town he has drawn incorporates on the fifth of February, 1851.
suggested_refs: The original 1850 town plat of Marysville, Yuba County, California

stops.name: Hyde Park, London: the Great Exhibition and the camera
stops.date_confidence: the Great Exhibition ran 1 May to 15 October 1851, which fixes the year; the standard account supplies no date at all for this episode. The tutelage under William Henry Fox Talbot is an uncited sentence resting on Le Plongeon's own telling and is treated here as reconstruction, not attestation
stops.campa: Inside the glass building in Hyde Park he sees photographic processes demonstrated and does not leave England again until he has learned them. He comes out of the country a photographer, and from that year he reckons exposure and light in front of every wall he means to record. He says afterward that he studied under William Henry Fox Talbot, the man who made the negative from which any number of prints can be pulled. No independent record confirms it. Whether he ever stood in Talbot's rooms, the reachable sources cannot say.
suggested_refs: The photographic exhibits of the Great Exhibition of 1851, Crystal Palace, Hyde Park

stops.name: St. Thomas, testing plates in the tropics
stops.date_confidence: attested that he tested photographic methods in tropical locations including St. Thomas, Mexico, Australia, China and the Pacific Islands. No source consulted supplies dates or an itinerary; the 1855 date orders the segment and is not a claim
stops.campa: A wet plate is a chemical accident waiting for heat, and heat is what the tropics have. He carries his apparatus to St. Thomas, to Mexico, to Australia, to China and the Pacific islands, testing which processes hold in humidity and which fog, bleach, or slide off the glass before the exposure is done. By the time he reaches Yucatan he knows which is which. No notebook from these years is reachable, no itinerary, no years: only the later plates, and the fact that they came out.
suggested_refs: Le Plongeon's own later accounts of tropical photographic trials, cited secondhand in the standard biography

stops.name: San Francisco, the Clay Street studio
stops.date_confidence: attested that he opened a daguerreotype studio in San Francisco in the 1850s; the year within the decade is not given in the sources consulted, and 1856 orders the segment
stops.campa: Back in San Francisco he opens a daguerreotype studio and makes portraits for money. The sitters are miners, merchants, women newly off the ships, people who want a plate to send home proving they exist and are prospering. It is the only stretch of his working life in which photography is a business rather than an instrument. He is not yet thirty-five and has been a teacher, a surveyor, a medical apprentice, and a shipwreck. He closes the studio and goes south.
suggested_refs: San Francisco city directories of the 1850s, Clay Street photographic galleries

segments.name: Eight Years on the Pacific Coast of South America

stops.name: Lima, the studio and the clinic on the Plaza Mayor
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1862; no month in the sources consulted. The coordinate is the Plaza Mayor of Lima, the city centre, not a located address for either the studio or the clinic
stops.campa: In 1862 he settles in Lima and opens two doors at once: a photographic studio, and a clinic practicing what his own century calls alternative medicine, electricity and water among its instruments. He will keep both for eight years. The two trades feed each other, since the clinic pays for the chemicals and the camera makes him, in the eyes of the people he photographs, something other than one more foreigner asking questions. Lima is the base, not the object. From it he rides out to whatever the Inca left standing.
suggested_refs: Lima photographic studio registers of the 1860s

stops.name: Tiwanaku, the ruins on the altiplano
stops.date_confidence: attested that he photographed Tiahuanaco during his South American years, 1862-1870; no year is given for the visit and 1864 orders the segment only. Note that Tiwanaku stands in Bolivia, not Peru: the standard phrase 'eight years in Peru photographing ruins including Tiahuanaco' silently annexes a Bolivian site
stops.campa: The great platform and the gateway stand on the Bolivian altiplano near Lake Titicaca, twelve thousand feet up, worked in stone fitted without mortar by people whose descendants the Spanish could get no account from. He photographs them. Here the idea arrives that will run the rest of his life: that ruins this old, this precise, and this unaccountable to any later inhabitant must be the work of a civilization the historians have not got. He is right about the gap. Everything he puts in it will be wrong.
stops.quote: all communications between their people and the inhabitants of the 'Lands of the West' had been interrupted for 9,000 years, in consequence of the great cataclysms, during which, in one night, the large island of Atlantis disappeared, submerged under the waves of the ocean.
stops.quote_source: Augustus Le Plongeon, Sacred Mysteries Among the Mayas and the Quiches (1886), rendering the account the Egyptian priests give Solon in Plato's Timaeus
suggested_refs: The Gateway of the Sun and the Akapana platform at Tiwanaku, Bolivia

stops.name: Lima, the books against the Jesuits
stops.date_confidence: attested, with a correction. The two anti-Jesuit books appeared in different years: La religion de Jesus comparada con las ensenanzas de la Iglesia (1867) and Los Jesuitas y el Peru (1869). An account giving a single 1867 date for both is wrong
stops.campa: He publishes in Spanish, in Peru, against the Society of Jesus: first a comparison of the religion of Jesus with the teachings of the Church, then a book on the Jesuits and Peru. The first appears in 1867, the second in 1869. They make him enemies in a Catholic country and establish early the pattern of the rest of his career. He arrives in a place, learns it faster than a visitor should, and publishes the conclusion the local authorities least want to read. In Peru the authority is the Church. In Yucatan it will be archaeology.
suggested_refs: Augustus Le Plongeon, La religion de Jesus comparada con las ensenanzas de la Iglesia (1867); Los Jesuitas y el Peru (1869)

stops.name: Arica, the earthquake and the wave
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The standard account says only that he observed the 1868 Arica earthquake and documented the damage; the earthquake's own record does not mention him, and phrasings such as 'witnessed' and 'interviewed survivors' are unsupported embellishments. The date is the earthquake's own, 13 August 1868
stops.campa: On the thirteenth of August, 1868, the ground under Arica moves and the sea comes in behind it, carrying the American warship Wateree inland and setting it down upright in the desert. Le Plongeon is on this coast and the destruction reaches his notice; how close he stood to it, the record does not say. What he does with a catastrophe is what he always does. The damage is photographed and described. He is by then six years into the eight he will spend on the Pacific coast of South America.
suggested_refs: The USS Wateree, carried inland by the tsunami of 13 August 1868 and left standing in the Atacama

stops.name: San Francisco, lecturing at the Academy
stops.date_confidence: attested that he lectured at the California Academy of Sciences in 1870. The coordinate is the Academy's downtown site at California and Dupont, now Grant Avenue, where its first museum opened in 1874; the Academy did not reach Golden Gate Park until 1916, so a park pin would be anachronistic. The 1870 lecture room itself is not identified in the sources consulted
stops.campa: He comes back north after eight years and stands up before the California Academy of Sciences with his South American photographs. This is the closest he ever gets to the front door of institutional science, and he walks in through it as a photographer, which is the one credential nobody disputes. The plates are evidence. The interpretation he attaches to them is already running ahead of what the plates show, and the men in the room are polite about it. He does not stay. Within a year he is in London reading Maya manuscripts.
suggested_refs: Proceedings of the California Academy of Sciences, 1870

segments.name: The Museum, the Marriage, and the Landing

stops.name: The British Museum, reading the Maya manuscripts
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1871; no month in the sources consulted
stops.campa: In 1871 he is in Bloomsbury working on Mesoamerican manuscripts, the surviving codices and the copies and commentaries built around them, all of it undeciphered. Nobody in the room can read a Maya glyph and everybody is guessing. He decides that he can read them, using a key assembled out of Egyptian and Hebrew letters and out of Charles Etienne Brasseur de Bourbourg's alphabet, itself a misreading. The decipherment is false. He will build twenty-five years of work on it and never doubt it once.
stops.quote: the mud spoken of by the Egyptian priests had settled in the course of centuries, and that the sea-weeds mentioned by Hamilco had ceased to be a barrier
stops.quote_source: Augustus Le Plongeon, Queen Moo and the Egyptian Sphinx (1896), preface, p. xiii
suggested_refs: The Maya codices and the Landa alphabet as held and copied in the British Museum's collections, 1871

stops.name: London, meeting Alice Dixon
stops.date_confidence: attested that they met in London in 1871; no month in the sources consulted. The PLACE is disputed: one account puts the meeting at a spiritualist seance, another at the British Museum while he was studying there. The contradiction is recorded, not resolved, and the coordinate is the generic London pin rather than either candidate site
stops.campa: Alice Dixon is nineteen, London-born, daughter of the photographer Henry Dixon, already trained on her father's plates. He is forty-six. Where they meet is told two ways, at a spiritualist seance or in the British Museum, and neither account yields to the other. What follows is not disputed. She becomes his wife and his working partner, the second pair of hands on every wet plate in Yucatan, and in time the author of her own books about the country.
suggested_refs: The photographic practice of Henry Dixon of London, in which Alice Dixon trained

stops.name: New York, the marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1873; no month, officiant or church named in the sources consulted. The age gap is twenty-six years, not the twenty-five sometimes given: he was born 4 May 1825, she 12 December 1851
stops.campa: They marry in New York in 1873, twenty-six years between them, and leave almost at once for Mexico. Twenty-three years later he will put her name alone on the front of the book that carries his whole theory, ahead of the title page and ahead of Queen Moo herself. The partnership is a working one before it is anything else. She carries the plates, coats them and develops them, learns Yucatec Maya alongside him, and keeps the journals and day books of the eleven years in the field.
stops.quote: TO MY WIFE, ALICE D. LE PLONGEON, MY CONSTANT COMPANION DURING MY EXPLORATIONS OF THE RUINED CITIES OF THE MAYAS
stops.quote_source: Augustus Le Plongeon, Queen Moo and the Egyptian Sphinx (1896), dedication page
suggested_refs: New York City marriage records for 1873

stops.name: Progreso, landing on the Yucatan coast
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Progreso was Yucatan's working port in 1873 and is the probable point of entry, but no source consulted names the port at which the couple landed, or the month
stops.campa: The peninsula they come to is a limestone shelf with no rivers, twenty-six years into a war between the Maya of the east and the Spanish-descended cities of the west that the maps of the period decline to admit is still running. The ruins they mean to photograph lie in country where a foreigner travels with an escort or does not travel. They land with cameras, glass, chemicals and a portable darkroom, none of it replaceable nearer than New York. Neither of them has yet seen a Maya building.
suggested_refs: The Caste War of Yucatan, 1847 onward, still unresolved at the couple's arrival

stops.name: Merida, yellow fever on the Plaza Grande
stops.date_confidence: attested that Alice fell ill with yellow fever on their arrival in Merida in 1873; no month in the sources consulted
stops.campa: In Merida, Alice takes the yellow fever, which in the Yucatan of the 1870s kills a good share of the Europeans it touches. He nurses her through it, practicing the medicine he learned without a school. The recovery costs them months and buys them a thing no other foreign expedition has: time in the city, and the decision to spend it learning Yucatec Maya from the people who speak it rather than working through interpreters. Both of them come out able to talk to the villagers whose land the ruins stand on.
suggested_refs: The Plaza Grande and cathedral of Merida, built from the dismantled Maya city of Ti'ho

stops.name: Uxmal, the first ruins
stops.date_confidence: attested. The first excursion out of Merida was a short visit to Uxmal, placed with the 1873 arrival and the recovery from fever; no month is given. A reported disagreement between the two standard accounts, one supposedly dating this visit 1875, does not survive checking: neither gives 1875
stops.campa: Their first trip out of Merida is to Uxmal, a reconnaissance of a few days at most. They explore and they photograph. The long facade of the Governor's Palace runs two hundred and fifty feet along its platform under a mosaic of cut stone, every piece of it fitted dry, without mortar. He has seen Tiahuanaco and now he has seen this, and he has already decided that one fact about the ancient world explains both. The few days settle the shape of the next eleven years.
suggested_refs: The Governor's Palace at Uxmal, longest stone facade of the Puuc region

stops.name: Chichen Itza, arriving under escort with the wet plates
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1875 for the journey to Chichen Itza with a military escort and the beginning of systematic wet collodion documentation; no month in the sources consulted. The coordinate is El Castillo, the site's centre
stops.campa: They reach Chichen Itza with a military escort, because the eastern half of the peninsula is held by Maya who have been at war with Merida since 1847. The site is forest with buildings inside it. He sets up the wet collodion process on the spot: coat the glass, sensitize it, expose it, develop it before it dries, all of it in heat, under insects, in a tent that has to be dark. Every plate is a race against evaporation. They will make hundreds of them.
stops.quote: I have illustrated this book with photographs taken in situ, drawings and plans according to actual, careful surveys, made by me, of the monuments.
stops.quote_source: Augustus Le Plongeon, Queen Moo and the Egyptian Sphinx (1896), preface, p. xx
suggested_refs: The wet collodion glass-plate process as practiced in the field, 1875

stops.name: The Platform of the Eagles and Jaguars, the statue in the ground
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1875. The coordinate is approximate: no per-structure coordinate is published for the platform, which stands immediately north-northwest of El Castillo. The accounts also differ on whether the statue lay buried beneath the platform or merely near it, and this is not resolved here
stops.campa: In November he digs and finds a man of stone lying on his back with his knees drawn up, head turned to one side, a shallow dish held on his belly. Nothing like it has been recorded before. He names it Chaacmol, which he reads as the paw swift like thunder, and takes it for the portrait of a Maya prince, brother and husband of a queen he calls Moo. The archaeology of the next century keeps the name, respelled chacmool, applies it to a whole class of such figures found from Tula to Michoacan, and drops everything else he says about it.
stops.quote: For instance, we find in them the history of certain personages who, after their death, became the gods most universally revered by the Egyptians, Isis and Osiris, whose earthly history, related by Wilkinson and other writers who regard it as a myth, corresponds exactly to that of Queen Moo and her brother-husband Prince Coh, whose charred heart was found by me, preserved in a stone urn, in his mausoleum at Chichen.
stops.quote_source: Augustus Le Plongeon, Queen Moo and the Egyptian Sphinx (1896), preface, p. xvii
suggested_refs: The chacmool form as later classified across Toltec and Maya sites, from Tula to Michoacan

stops.name: The Platform of Venus, the sculptured record
stops.date_confidence: attested that he excavated the Platform of the Eagles and Jaguars and documented the Platform of Venus in 1875; no month in the sources consulted for the second
stops.campa: He clears and photographs the low platform later archaeologists will name for Venus, reading its carved panels as a chronicle: a court, a murder, a queen's flight. In the friezes of Chichen Itza he sees a continuous narrative nobody else can see, because the glyphs are not readable and the figures can be made to mean whatever a determined reader needs them to mean. The photographs he takes here are exact. They are still consulted, because much of what he photographed has since weathered off the stone.
stops.quote: On the top of the monument was his totem, a dying leopard with a human head, a veritable sphinx.
stops.quote_source: Augustus Le Plongeon, Queen Moo and the Egyptian Sphinx (1896)
suggested_refs: The Platform of Venus and the Platform of the Eagles and Jaguars, Chichen Itza, as photographed 1875

stops.name: Uxmal, the Pyramid of the Magician
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The photographing of the Pyramid of the Magician is reported without a firm date; 1876 is taken from the couple's Uxmal work of that period and orders the segment
stops.campa: The pyramid at Uxmal has an oval base, a stair so steep it is climbed on hands as much as feet, and a temple doorway carved as the open jaws of the rain god. Between them, he and Alice record Uxmal and Chichen Itza on glass more fully than anyone has recorded a Maya site to that date. He photographs the pyramid from below and from across the quadrangle, working the light through the hours it takes for the shadow to leave the facade. Alice works beside him, coating the next plate.
suggested_refs: The Pyramid of the Magician, Uxmal, and its Chenes-style temple doorway

stops.name: The Centennial grounds, Philadelphia: the statue refused
stops.date_confidence: attested that he sought permission to display the Chacmool at the 1876 Centennial Exhibition and that the request was refused. No source consulted places Le Plongeon himself on the Exhibition grounds: the petition is attested, the travel is not. The date is the Exhibition's opening month
stops.campa: He wants the stone man in Philadelphia, in front of the crowds the United States has assembled to look at its own first century, and he asks permission to ship it there. The answer is no. The statue he dug out of the ground at his own expense is not his to move, a point Mexico is about to make in a way he cannot argue with. Three years and most of the Marysville money have gone into the peninsula by now, and the peninsula is not going to let him keep anything he finds. The Centennial opens without it.
suggested_refs: The Centennial Exhibition, Fairmount Park, Philadelphia, 10 May to 10 November 1876

stops.name: Izamal, the pyramid of Kinich Kakmo
stops.date_confidence: attested that the couple visited and photographed Izamal. The standard account dates the whole set of secondary sites to the span 1873 to 1884 and gives no individual years, so the date here orders the segment only
stops.campa: At Izamal the Franciscans built their monastery on top of a Maya platform and out of its stone, and the pyramid of Kinich Kakmo still stands over the town, a hill of dressed blocks with houses at its foot. He gets the colonial church and the pyramid into a single frame. One civilization stands on the flattened top of another and the second is still plainly there underneath, holding the first one up. He finds the same arrangement everywhere on the peninsula, and photographs it wherever the light allows.
suggested_refs: The Convento de San Antonio de Padua at Izamal, raised on the Maya acropolis

stops.name: Mayapan, the walled city
stops.date_confidence: attested as one of the sites the couple worked; no individual year is given in the sources consulted, the whole group being dated 1873-1884. The date orders the segment
stops.campa: Mayapan was the last capital to hold a league of Maya cities together, and it came apart in the fifteenth century, before any European saw it standing. What is left inside its wall is a small shabby copy of Chichen Itza: a shrunken Castillo, a round tower, house mounds by the hundred. Nothing on this site supports a civilization eleven thousand five hundred years old, and nothing on it is permitted to disturb one. The Le Plongeons photograph the platforms and measure the wall.
suggested_refs: The city wall and Castillo of Mayapan, abandoned c. 1450

stops.name: Ake, the megalithic colonnade
stops.date_confidence: attested as one of the sites visited; no year is given, so the date orders the segment within the 1873-1884 span. Coordinate corrected: Ake stands about forty kilometres east of Merida in the municipality of Tixkokob, not on the city's edge
stops.campa: Ake is a platform carrying thirty-five columns of rough megalithic stone in rows, heavier and cruder than anything at Uxmal, and old, though nobody in 1877 can say how old. He surveys it. Columns without capitals, without carving, without a glyph on them: a site that gives a reader nothing to read, which for once leaves his method with nothing to work on. A hacienda works the land around the stones and the henequen goes out past them by the cartload.
suggested_refs: The megalithic colonnade of Ake, Tixkokob, Yucatan

stops.name: Belize City, south out of the peninsula
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1878 for the journey south into British Honduras before returning to the United States to seek funding; no month in the sources consulted
stops.campa: In 1878 they go south into British Honduras, out of Mexico and into a British colony of mahogany cutters on a swamp at a river mouth. It is the far end of the survey and the end of the money. He has been working the peninsula for five years on the proceeds of a California land deal and there is nothing left of it. From here they turn north to the United States to look for a sponsor, carrying plate negatives, drawings, and plaster molds of the sculpture they cannot carry itself.
suggested_refs: Belize City in 1878, capital of the mahogany colony of British Honduras

stops.name: Isla Mujeres, the shrine on the point
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The island is named among the sites visited; the identification of the structure as the shrine of Ixchel and the year are both inferences, the group of sites being dated collectively 1873-1884
stops.campa: On the southern point of the island, on a low cliff over the Caribbean, stands a small square building the Spanish took for a temple of the moon goddess Ixchel, to whom Maya women crossed the water to make offerings about childbirth. He photographs it. The couple are working the eastern coast now, the least visited edge of the peninsula, where the ruins stand within sound of the sea and the war has never quite stopped. They travel by boat, because the interior roads do not come here.
suggested_refs: The shrine at Punta Sur, Isla Mujeres, identified as a temple of Ixchel

stops.name: Cozumel, the ruins on the island
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The sources name Cozumel generically; identifying the ruins he surveyed as San Gervasio is an inference, and the year orders the segment within the collective 1873-1884 span
stops.campa: Cozumel was a pilgrimage island before the conquest and a smugglers' anchorage after it, and its ruins sit inland under low forest, small buildings on low platforms, plastered once and painted. He records what he finds. The plates from these coastal seasons are less spectacular than Chichen Itza and more useful, because nobody else is making any: for most of the eastern sites, a Le Plongeon negative is the earliest image that exists. He is fifty-six years old and carrying his own glass through the forest.
suggested_refs: The San Gervasio group, Cozumel, sanctuary of Ixchel and pre-conquest pilgrimage destination

stops.name: Cancun, the ruins at El Rey
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The sources name Cancun generically; El Rey is an inference, its coordinate is approximate and unconfirmed against INAH, and the year orders the segment within the 1873-1884 span
stops.campa: Cancun in 1882 is a sandbar between a lagoon and the sea with a small ruined settlement on it, temples and platforms of a fishing and trading community, and almost nobody living there. He photographs it and leaves. A century later the sandbar will carry a city of hotels built the length of the same strip, and the ruins will sit in the middle of it behind a fence, and the plates he made when there was nothing else on the sand will be the record of what the place was.
suggested_refs: The El Rey group, Cancun, on the lagoon side of the barrier island

segments.name: The Statue Taken and the Search for Sponsors

stops.name: Merida, the Chacmool seized
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1877 for the seizure by the Yucatecan government and the handover to the federal government, which moved the statue to Mexico City; no month in the sources consulted
stops.campa: The government of Yucatan takes the statue. It is hauled to Merida, and Yucatan hands it to the federal government, which sends it on to the capital, where it goes into the national collection and stays. He had meant to take it to Philadelphia and after that, by his own account, to New York, and he never accepts that a state has a prior claim on what is dug out of its ground. The quarrel follows him the rest of his career and costs him the goodwill of every Mexican official he needs.
suggested_refs: Mexican federal claims over antiquities removed from Yucatan, asserted 1877

stops.name: Worcester, elected to the American Antiquarian Society
stops.date_confidence: attested that he was elected a member in 1878; no source consulted records him travelling to Worcester. The coordinate is the Society's Salisbury Street building, completed only in 1910, so the address is anachronistic for the election year, when the Society occupied its earlier Lincoln Square premises
stops.campa: The American Antiquarian Society elects him a member in 1878, the high-water mark of his standing among American scholars. It comes for the photographs and the excavation rather than for the theory, which is barely in print yet. Within a decade the same body of men will regard him as a crank. He loses no argument in those years; the field acquires standards of excavation and evidence, and he declines to meet them. Whether he ever set foot in Worcester the record does not say.
suggested_refs: Proceedings of the American Antiquarian Society, membership elections of 1878

stops.name: Mexico City, four years in the capital
stops.date_confidence: attested that the couple spent time in Mexico City from 1880 to 1884, not from 1877: 1877 is the year of the seizure, not of their residence. The coordinate is the nineteenth-century Museo Nacional on Calle de Moneda beside the National Palace; the National Museum of Anthropology in Chapultepec, where the statue stands today, did not open until 1964 and is a different institution
stops.campa: From 1880 to 1884 they are in the capital, contesting the handling of the Chacmool, applying for permits, and looking for money that never arrives from anywhere. The statue sits in the Museo Nacional on Calle de Moneda, minutes on foot from wherever they are lodging, and he can go and look at it whenever he likes. He cannot photograph it on his own terms, publish it as his own find, or move it. He goes on excavating on the peninsula between trips to the capital.
suggested_refs: The Museo Nacional on Calle de Moneda, Mexico City, holder of the Chacmool from 1877

segments.name: Queen Moo and the Mother of Nations

stops.name: New York, Vestiges of the Mayas
stops.date_confidence: attested: Vestiges of the Mayas, New York, 1881. Correction to a common gloss: it is a short pamphlet reporting the Yucatan fieldwork, and the Egypt and Atlantis thesis is not in it. That belongs to Sacred Mysteries (1886) and Queen Moo (1896)
stops.campa: The first book is a pamphlet, and it is mostly fieldwork: what he dug, where, and what he photographed. The apparatus of Queen Moo, the drowned continent and the Egyptian succession is not yet in print. At this point he is still a man with an unmatched photographic record of two Maya cities and an eccentric reading of them, and it is the record the reviewers notice. He is fifty-six. He publishes it himself, in New York, between campaigns on the peninsula.
suggested_refs: Augustus Le Plongeon, Vestiges of the Mayas (New York, 1881)

stops.name: New York, the name Mu
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The derivation of Mu from Brasseur de Bourbourg's 1864 misreading of the Madrid Codex, and the placing of the land in the Atlantic, are reported without a firm date; 1884 orders the segment. Note the direction of influence: the Atlantic siting follows Ignatius Donnelly's Atlantis: The Antediluvian World (1882), so Le Plongeon borrowed from Donnelly as well as the reverse
stops.campa: The abbe Charles Etienne Brasseur de Bourbourg had years before run the Landa alphabet against the Madrid Codex and produced from it a syllable he read as the name of a drowned country: Mu. The alphabet was wrong and so was the reading. Le Plongeon takes the word, gives the country a queen, and places it in the Atlantic, following Ignatius Loyola Donnelly, whose Atlantis: The Antediluvian World came out in 1882 and set the whole English-speaking world arguing about a continent.
stops.quote: several pages at the beginning of the second part are dedicated to the recital of the awful phenomena that took place during the cataclysm that caused the submersion of ten countries, among which the 'Land of Mu,' that large island probably called 'Atlantis' by Plato
stops.quote_source: Augustus Le Plongeon, Queen Moo and the Egyptian Sphinx (1896), introduction, p. xli
suggested_refs: Charles Etienne Brasseur de Bourbourg's 1864 reading of the Madrid Codex, source of the syllable Mu
Ignatius Loyola Donnelly, Atlantis: The Antediluvian World (1882)

stops.name: New York, Sacred Mysteries Among the Mayas and the Quiches
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1886, New York, for both books named here
stops.campa: The second book puts the whole claim on the page: that the religious rites of Egypt, of the Euphrates and of the shores of the Indian Ocean were carried there by Maya colonists eleven thousand five hundred years ago, and that Freemasonry, whose degrees he reads into the Chichen Itza friezes, descends from the same source. In the same year Alice publishes Here and There in Yucatan, an account of the country and the people they have been living among for thirteen years.
stops.quote: I will try to trace their origin, step by step, to this continent which we inhabit, to America, from where Maya colonists transported their ancient religious rites and ceremonies, not only to the banks of the Nile, but to those of the Euphrates, and the shores of the Indian Ocean, not less than 11,500 years ago.
stops.quote_source: Augustus Le Plongeon, Sacred Mysteries Among the Mayas and the Quiches (1886)
suggested_refs: Alice Dixon Le Plongeon, Here and There in Yucatan (New York, 1886)

stops.name: New York, the theory against the field
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. His marginalization among professional archaeologists as evidence accumulated against cultural diffusion is reported without dates; 1890 orders the segment. Blavatsky's use of his Maya material is attested; the reverse direction, him drawing on her, is not claimed by any source consulted
stops.campa: The field turns. Americanist archaeology in the 1880s and 1890s is becoming a profession with stratigraphy, controlled excavation, and a standing objection to anyone who explains a New World civilization by an Old World arrival. Le Plongeon answers that his opponents have never been to Yucatan, which is true, and that he has read the glyphs, which is not. Helena Blavatsky, drawing on his Maya material for the lost-continent doctrine of Theosophy, goes on citing him after the archaeologists have stopped.
stops.quote: Mayach, not India, is the true mother of nations.
stops.quote_source: Augustus Le Plongeon, Queen Moo and the Egyptian Sphinx (1896)
suggested_refs: Helena Blavatsky's use of Le Plongeon's Maya material in the Theosophical lost-continent doctrine

segments.name: Brooklyn, the Last Defence, and After

stops.name: Brooklyn, the house of the defence
stops.date_confidence: attested that he spent his remaining years in Brooklyn writing about the supposed Maya-Egypt connection and defending his theories; the sources consulted give no address and no year of removal, so the date orders the segment
stops.campa: He is sixty-five and he is finished with the field. The rest is Brooklyn: the plates in their boxes, the drawings, the molds, the correspondence with the men who still answer, and the writing. Alice writes beside him. Neither of them will see Yucatan again. Between them they hold the most complete photographic record of Chichen Itza and Uxmal in existence, and the reason nobody will use it for fifty years is the theory it comes attached to. He goes on defending the theory. He has never once conceded a point of it in writing.
stops.quote: the ancient sacred mysteries, the origin of Free Masonry consequently, date back from a period far more remote than the most sanguine students of its history ever imagined.
stops.quote_source: Augustus Le Plongeon, Sacred Mysteries Among the Mayas and the Quiches (1886)
suggested_refs: The Le Plongeon papers and glass negatives as assembled in Brooklyn, 1890-1908

stops.name: New York, Queen Moo and the Egyptian Sphinx
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1896; title and date drawn from the standard bibliography. The quoted Isis and Osiris passage is given here as it actually reads in the preface, p. xvii, a version of it circulating in spliced form having been checked against the scan and rejected
stops.campa: The book of his life comes out in 1896, dedicated to his wife, illustrated from his own negatives, and built entirely on a decipherment that does not work. Queen Moo flees the wreck of her country eastward, reaches the Maya colonies established on the Nile, is received as the Little Sister, iolu, Isis, and is proclaimed their queen. Her brother-husband Prince Coh becomes Osiris. The charred heart in the stone urn at Chichen is Coh's, found by him. Every element of it is false and every photograph in it is good.
stops.quote: Fleeing from the wrath of her brother Aac, Queen Moo directed her course toward the rising sun...she continued her journey eastward, and at last reached the Maya colonies that for many years had been established on the banks of the Nile. The settlers received her with open arms, called her the 'Little sister,' iolu (Isis), and proclaimed her their queen.
stops.quote_source: Augustus Le Plongeon, Queen Moo and the Egyptian Sphinx (1896)
suggested_refs: Augustus Le Plongeon, Queen Moo and the Egyptian Sphinx (New York, 1896), preface, p. xvii, on Isis, Osiris and Prince Coh
sources: Augustus Le Plongeon, Queen Moo and the Egyptian Sphinx (1896)

stops.name: Brooklyn, Queen Moo's Talisman
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1902 for Alice Dixon Le Plongeon's epic poem Queen Moo's Talisman, published in New York while Augustus was living
stops.campa: Alice puts the story into verse. Queen Moo's Talisman is an epic poem on the same drowned country, the same flight, the same queen, published in New York in 1902 while he is alive to read it. She is fifty that year and he is seventy-seven. By then the theory has left archaeology altogether and entered literature, and literature is where it travels: through Theosophy, through the Atlantis books, through the occult presses. The professionals stopped answering his letters years ago.
suggested_refs: Alice Dixon Le Plongeon, Queen Moo's Talisman (New York, 1902)

stops.name: Brooklyn, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested: died at Brooklyn, 13 December 1908, aged eighty-three, his health having declined through that year. Gap: no source consulted records his burial place or any grave marker, and none is invented here
stops.campa: His health goes through 1908 and he dies in Brooklyn on the thirteenth of December, eighty-three years old. Sixty-four years before, he had come ashore off a wrecked ship on the coast of Chile with nothing at all. Alice is fifty-six and has been at his side for thirty-five years, on the plaza at Merida, in the tent darkroom at Chichen Itza, in boats along the Quintana Roo coast, and in the Brooklyn house. She is left with the plates, the manuscripts, and the theory to defend by herself. Where he is buried, no reachable source says.
suggested_refs: Brooklyn burial records for December 1908, not located in the sources consulted

stops.name: New York, the end of the partnership
stops.date_confidence: attested: diagnosed with breast cancer February 1910, died 8 June 1910 at the New York Women's Hospital. Age corrected: she was 58, not 59, having been born 12 December 1851. Her serial A Dream of Atlantis ran in The World Magazine from 1909 to 1911, beginning after his death and finishing after hers. The traveller at this stop is Alice, not Augustus; it is placed here because it closes the joint archive
stops.campa: She outlives him by eighteen months. In those months her serial A Dream of Atlantis begins running in The World Magazine, the last of the Queen Moo material to reach a general readership. It is still appearing when she is diagnosed with breast cancer in February 1910, and it goes on appearing for a year after her. She dies on the eighth of June at the New York Women's Hospital, fifty-eight years old. The plates, the notebooks, the drawings and the plaster molds pass out of the family's hands.
suggested_refs: Alice Dixon Le Plongeon, 'A Dream of Atlantis', serialized in The World Magazine, 1909-1911

stops.name: New York, Mu moved to the Pacific
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1926 for James Churchward's The Lost Continent of Mu, the Motherland of Man. This stop is posthumous, recording the descent of Le Plongeon's own material eighteen years after his death; Le Plongeon is not present at it and Churchward is not on record having met him
stops.campa: James Churchward takes the word Mu, moves the continent from the Atlantic to the Pacific, populates it with sixty-four million people and seven cities, and sells it in editions still in print a century later. He does not need Chichen Itza, the negatives, or the eleven years in the field; the name is enough. What Le Plongeon dug out of the ground and photographed at his own expense comes apart here from what he made up, and it is the invention that sells. Churchward is not on record as ever having met him.
stops.quote: Of this dreadful cataclysm, in which perished sixty-four millions of human beings, four different authors have left descriptions in the Maya language.
stops.quote_source: Augustus Le Plongeon, Queen Moo and the Egyptian Sphinx (1896), preface, p. xviii
suggested_refs: James Churchward, The Lost Continent of Mu, the Motherland of Man (1926)

stops.name: Los Angeles, the plates in the Getty
stops.date_confidence: attested that the couple's glass-plate photographic archive of Chichen Itza, Uxmal and Mayapan is held at the Getty Research Institute, Los Angeles. No acquisition date is given in the sources consulted; the 1980 date orders the closing stop and is not a claim. The coordinate is the canonical Los Angeles pin, not the Institute's Brentwood address
stops.campa: The glass negatives of Chichen Itza, Uxmal and Mayapan are at the Getty Research Institute in Los Angeles, catalogued, conserved and consulted. They show buildings, friezes and inscriptions as they stood in the 1870s, before a century and a half of rain, tourists and restoration, and in a number of cases they are the only record of surfaces that no longer exist. The archaeology he set out to overturn now uses his photographs as primary evidence and his conclusions as nothing at all.
suggested_refs: The Augustus and Alice Dixon Le Plongeon papers and photographs, Getty Research Institute, Los Angeles
